title: India needs 2.9 mn additional hospital beds by 2035 to meet the global benchmark: CBRE
summary: Healthcare investment increasingly shifting towards specialised facilities, day-care formats and acquisition-led expansion

contentHtml:
Healthcare investment increasingly shifting towards specialised facilities, day-care formats and acquisition-led expansion

India is projected to require an additional 2.6 bn. sq. ft. of healthcare real estate by 2035, driven by the need for nearly 2.9 million incremental hospital beds, to align with the current global healthcare infrastructure benchmark, according to CBRE South Asia’s latest report titled “Beyond Core: A 2035 View of India’s Alternate Sectors – Part I”.

India currently has approximately 1.6 hospital beds per 1,000 people, significantly below the global average of 3.3 per 1,000. To close this capacity gap, the country’s total healthcare real estate footprint would need to expand substantially from an estimated 2.1 bn. sq. ft. in 2025, the report highlights. The requirement presents a significant opportunity for developers, investors and healthcare operators to create purpose-built and scalable healthcare assets across markets.

The report’s analysis of non-communicable disease (NCD) prevalence and hospital bed density highlights significant disparities in healthcare infrastructure across states. Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand have low hospital bed density compared with their disease burden, indicating potential unmet demand for secondary and tertiary healthcare services. Meanwhile, states such as Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana have relatively stronger healthcare infrastructure and higher household incomes, supporting further expansion of specialised healthcare facilities and medical ecosystems.

“Healthcare is emerging as one of India’s most consequential real estate opportunities, not simply because demand for care is increasing, but because the country needs a far deeper and more distributed physical healthcare network,” said Anshuman Magazine, Chairman and CEO, India, South-East Asia, Middle East and Africa, CBRE.

He added, “Built-to-suit (BTS) structures can play an important role in addressing this requirement by providing operators with specialised, purpose-built clinical infrastructure aligned with their operational and regulatory needs. This would allow healthcare providers to direct more capital towards clinical services, medical equipment and technology, while offering property owners greater income visibility through long-term leases.”

Beyond conventional hospitals, the sector is also witnessing the growth of diagnostic centres, day-care surgery centres, wellness and preventive healthcare formats, including health screening centres, rehabilitation clinics, eye-care centres, IVF centres and vaccination facilities, particularly in urban locations.

The report identifies a shift in healthcare investment and expansion strategies, with growing interest in single-speciality hospitals, day-care and outpatient facilities, and acquisition-led expansion. Given the highly competitive landscape in certain cities, operators are increasingly evaluating existing hospitals to enter established markets faster, leveraging operational infrastructure, licences and patient networks.

Although nascent, medical office buildings can also be developed in the country, housing single or multiple healthcare tenants such as diagnostics, rehabilitation, child development, IVF, eye-care, dental and wellness providers. These assets allow multiple services to be co-located within one development, improving patient convenience while strengthening asset utilisation.

“India’s healthcare infrastructure requirement cannot be addressed through a uniform development model,” said Rami Kaushal, Managing Director, Consulting and Valuation Services, India, Middle East and Africa, CBRE. “The current landscape creates scope for a diversified development pipeline, ranging from large integrated healthcare campuses and multi- and single-speciality hospitals to medical office buildings, diagnostics and day-care facilities. In addition to top cities, tier-II and tier-III locations are particularly important in this context, where lower land costs and the availability of larger parcels can support cost-efficient, purpose-built healthcare developments.”
